Introduction

I recently took over an end-of-line (EOL) testing project that uses Gaussian mixture models (GMMs) for quality inspection of products on the production line. Feature extraction was painful, but the work is a lot of fun. Out of curiosity, I also took Andrew Ng’s Machine Learning course on Coursera last year, which served as my introduction to the field. With machine learning on the rise, every discipline is eagerly jumping on the bandwagon and looking for where it fits in. In this series I’ll talk about how machine learning is being applied in acoustics. The title is a little grandiose and could be accused of riding the AI hype; really, it is mostly about machine learning. My knowledge of machine learning is limited, so discussion and corrections are very welcome.

Background

Machine learning is now widely used in computer vision, image processing, speech processing, geophysics and other fields. As with other techniques, such as compressive sensing, machine learning first caused a stir in computing and image processing, and only then began to make its mark in acoustics. Acoustics came to it late, but progress has been fast. It is already applied in subfields such as human speech, animal vocalizations and underwater source localization.

Most readers will have some idea of what machine learning is. Broadly, it can be defined as the use of computers to study algorithms and statistical models that perform a specific task without explicit instructions, relying instead on patterns and features in the data [1]. Machine learning falls into three broad categories: supervised learning, unsupervised learning and reinforcement learning. In this article we focus on the first two.

Professor Andrew Ng defines supervised learning as follows:

In supervised learning, we are given a data set and already know what our correct output should look like, having the idea that there is a relationship between the input and the output [2].

And unsupervised learning:

Unsupervised learning allows us to approach problems with little or no idea what our results should look like. We can derive structure from data where we don’t necessarily know the effect of the variables.

Put simply, in supervised learning we already have expectations about the output and know what it looks like; in unsupervised learning we don’t know what the output should be, and we let the data decide. Take classification: sorting spam email is supervised learning, while grouping similar news stories together is unsupervised learning, because we don’t know how many groups there should be, nor do we have specific criteria for them.

Acoustics is a branch of physics, and for centuries people have worked on developing its physical models, as shown along the x-axis of the figure below. As data volumes have grown, data-driven methods have gradually come into use as well, shown along the y-axis. The top right corner is where acoustics is heading: more advanced and complete physical models combined with machine learning driven by big data [3]. In machine learning, the features of the data are key.

Common machine learning methods

There is a vast amount of material out there for learning machine learning, and as an outsider I won’t presume to lecture on the basics. Here I’ll just list a few of the more commonly used methods.

Supervised learning

1. Regression and classification

Here is a figure from Andrew Ng’s Machine Learning course on Coursera that shows what regression is. The x-axis is the floor area of a house and the y-axis its price. We can fit various curves to represent the price trend, and so predict the price from the area.

[Machine Learning, Coursera]

Classification is easy to grasp. A simple example:

[Machine Learning, Coursera]

Other methods include support vector machines (SVMs) and neural networks. SVMs are more flexible than regression, and neural networks can use nonlinear models for prediction or classification.

Nonlinear classification with a neural network [Machine Learning, Coursera]

Unsupervised learning

The main methods are:

1. Principal component analysis (PCA)

PCA: an orthogonal transformation converts the data into linearly uncorrelated principal components, hitting the data with a “dimensional strike” (to borrow from The Three-Body Problem) so that the features become more representative [Wikipedia]

2. K-means

K-means: iteratively finds the center of each cluster of data and classifies the data accordingly [Wikipedia]

3. GMM and expectation maximization (EM)

Like k-means, this is a form of cluster analysis. It classifies features by mixing several different Gaussian distributions.

GMM [https://towardsdatascience.com/gaussian-mixture-models-explained-6986aaf5a95]

Other methods include dictionary learning, autoencoder networks and deep learning (including convolutional neural networks).

Applications of machine learning in acoustics

1. Source localization in audio processing

In audio processing, enhancing the speech of a source or talker is the core problem. The combination of acoustics and machine learning is widely used in phones, cars, hearing aids and smart homes. Although the field is moving very fast, accurately identifying sources amid high background noise and room reverberation remains the biggest challenge. The LOCATA project recently launched a challenge on acoustic source localization and tracking, and built a corpus of real-life recordings for training localization algorithms [4]. Speech technology companies in China and abroad are all working on this.

GMM combined with EM improves localization accuracy [3]

2. Source localization in ocean acoustics

Source localization in the ocean relies mainly on sonar systems combined with matched field processing (MFP). Because sound sources are almost always sparsely distributed in space (space isn’t packed full of sources), compressive sensing was brought into acoustics over the past decade or so. As mentioned above, acoustics usually adopts new techniques from other disciplines with some delay; that seems to be a trait of the field.

Neural networks have been used to locate cargo ships accurately [5]. For shallow and sloping ocean environments, time delay neural network (TDNN) models need to be trained for different water depths to avoid mismatch [6]. This year, researchers also succeeded in predicting source range and depth using a single hydrophone combined with a deep residual CNN (ResNet) [7]. As computing power grows (quantum computers, for example, though who knows how many years before they are commercially available), combining machine learning with physical models should make more accurate real-time source localization in the ocean possible.

Spectrograms of three ships at different times [5]

3. Bioacoustics

This is a particularly interesting area of application. Bioacoustics studies how living creatures in nature produce and perceive all kinds of sounds, not just vocalizations. Machine learning has already been used to tackle questions such as: Why do animals make sounds? Why did calls and songs evolve? How are these sounds related? There is a wealth of data on all of this for machine learning to work with.

By recording animal calls, researchers can classify the biological and ecological behavior of animals, and from that determine how densely an area is populated, how that density changes over time, how the phases of the moon affect foraging, and so on. As early as the 1990s, researchers characterized the sounds of marine animals, training machine learning models on psychoacoustic parameters, time–frequency features and other features extracted from the audio. In the 1980s, dolphin species were already being classified by their calls. Later, GMMs were used to study how the spectral parameters of toothed-whale calls vary; hidden Markov models (HMMs) were used to identify birds by their song; and multilayer neural networks were used to classify bats and whales, and to recognize the calls of killer whales, handy for knowing when to make a run for it. Ensemble learning has even been used to classify bumblebees. Unsupervised learning has not yet been widely used in bioacoustics.

A few interesting bioacoustics databases:

https://www.macaulaylibrary.org

Sharing bird sounds from around the world

MobySound.org

British Library - Sounds

https://www.ngdc.noaa.gov/mgg/pad/

Machine learning and acoustics are also being combined in medicine for diagnosis. Noisy Guts in Australia (http://www.noisyguts.net/), for example, uses acoustic signals and machine learning to diagnose bowel disorders.

There is also emotion analysis of speech signals, which picks up vocal signs of imminent dangerous behavior so that people can step in early and prevent violence. It could be used in places such as kindergartens and prisons. A company in the Netherlands is working on exactly this.

The spectrogram shows a sudden, dramatic change in the person’s voice [https://www.soundintel.com/products/overview/aggression/]

4. Geological exploration

Seismic exploration for hydrocarbons works mainly by recording reflections of emitted seismic waves and analyzing whether the reflecting layers below the surface show discontinuities, which reveals whether hydrocarbon resources lie underground. The traditional approach in this field combines signal and image processing; using acoustics for geological exploration is a recent development.

5. Reverberation and environmental sound

Every day, people deal with complex acoustic environments full of all sorts of sources: speech, music, impacts, friction, flow, animals, machines and more. The sound from each source interacts with other sources and with the surroundings, so what reaches our ears is very complex and no longer contains the original sound of any one source. As mentioned earlier, removing reverberation and reflections, and extracting the source signal from a mixture, are open challenges for acoustics combined with machine learning. We need hearing aids, for instance, that can pick out voices from background noise, and self-driving cars that can hear a siren on a noisy street and pull over (though in China, I suspect, that feature wouldn’t get much use).

Identifying sources in natural environments faces several problems:

there are many kinds of sources;

each kind of source varies enormously;

in natural environments, many sound events happen at the same time and interfere with one another.

There are now plenty of databases of natural recordings for training classifiers, such as the DCASE challenges, ESC, TUT, AudioSet, and urban sound and scene classification sets (DCASE; TUT).

Combining acoustics with advanced image processing to classify acoustic scenes and identify sources can improve recognition. Physical models can also be used to simulate sounds, making it easy to generate more data for feature extraction and model training [9].

Synthesizing a large contrastive sound database with physical models [9]

Main reference: Machine learning in acoustics: theory and applications. JASA, 2019.
